note: The continuous half of Advanced Y12 random variables (8) + what Advanced adds to the normal distribution (3) + the Bernoulli and binomial half of Extension 1 Y12 binomial distributions (9) = 20. ORDER: needs W4-6 (discrete distributions, expectation and variance) and W4-5 (integration of the functions a pdf uses). The seven SHARED normal-distribution skills (`normal-distribution-shape`, `calculate-z-score`, `z-score-to-raw-score`, `compare-z-scores`, `empirical-rule`, `normal-probabilities`, `z-table-probability`) carry both a Standard and an Advanced dot point and are generated in W4-3 — they must NOT be re-queued here.

sections.name: continuous-random-variables
hazards: One routine per skill. `continuous-random-variable` = what makes a variable continuous, why $P(X=a)=0$, and why $P(X<a)=P(X\le a)$. `probability-density-function` = the two conditions ($f(x)\ge0$ everywhere, total area $1$), and computing $P(a<X<b)=\int_{a}^{b}f(x)dx$. `cumulative-distribution-function` = $F(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x}f(t)dt$, its properties (non-decreasing, from $0$ to $1$), recovering $f$ by differentiating $F$, and using $F$ to get interval probabilities. `pdf-unknown-constant` = finding $k$ from $\int f=1$.

A DENSITY IS NOT A PROBABILITY: $f(2)=0.4$ does NOT mean $P(X=2)=0.4$, and $f(x)$ MAY EXCEED 1. Both misreadings are compulsory named distractors, and at least one pdf in the section must take values above $1$ so the point is unavoidable.

$P(X=a)=0$ FOR A CONTINUOUS VARIABLE, so strict and non-strict inequalities give the same probability. Include an item that turns on exactly that, and never offer two options that differ only by a strict/non-strict boundary.

THE PDF IS ZERO OUTSIDE ITS STATED SUPPORT. Every $f$ must be written piecewise with its domain, and every integral's limits must be intersected with that support — integrating $\frac{3}{8}x^{2}$ from $0$ to $5$ when the support is $[0,2]$ is the section's dominant wrong-key defect. Check every limit against the support before keying.

VERIFY $\int f=1$ FOR EVERY DENSITY YOU WRITE, in every skill, including after solving for $k$. A pdf whose total area is not exactly $1$ makes every derived answer wrong while remaining internally consistent.

EVERY ITEM CARRIES A `[tikz]` FIGURE of the density with the relevant interval shaded. Plot as a function with `domain=` set to the support and clipped to the axis window; never `^` inside a plotted expression (write `exp(-x)`, not `e^(-x)`), and draw a piecewise density as separate restricted plots with the zero pieces drawn along the axis. Do not label the shaded area's value on a question figure.
$F(x)$ AND $f(x)$ MUST NEVER APPEAR IN THE SAME OPTION LIST without the stem saying which is wanted — they are different functions and both are 'the answer' to a careless stem.

sections.name: continuous-measures
hazards: One routine per skill. `continuous-uniform-distribution` = $f(x)=\frac{1}{b-a}$ on $[a,b]$, its probabilities as rectangle areas, and its mean $\frac{a+b}{2}$ and variance $\frac{(b-a)^{2}}{12}$. `mean-variance-continuous` = $\mu=\int xf(x)dx$ and $\sigma^{2}=\int x^{2}f(x)dx-\mu^{2}$. `median-quartiles-continuous` = solving $F(m)=0.5$ (and $0.25$, $0.75$). `mode-continuous-distribution` = the $x$ that MAXIMISES $f$, found by calculus or by inspection, including a mode at an endpoint of the support.

THE MEDIAN SOLVES $F(m)=0.5$, NOT $f(m)=0.5$ AND NOT $\frac{a+b}{2}$ IN GENERAL. All three confusions must appear as named distractors, and at least half the `median-quartiles-continuous` items must have a SKEWED density so the median differs from the mean and from the midpoint of the support.

THE MODE IS A MAXIMUM OF THE DENSITY, so it needs $f'=0$ AND a check that it is a maximum, or an endpoint comparison. A density that is monotonic on its support has its mode at an ENDPOINT — include one such item, since 'solved $f'=0$ and got a value outside the support' is the compulsory named distractor.

$\sigma^{2}=E(X^{2})-\mu^{2}$, AND THE $\mu^{2}$ IS SUBTRACTED ONCE. Forgetting it is the compulsory named distractor for `mean-variance-continuous`; check every variance is POSITIVE before keying — a negative variance means the arithmetic is wrong, and it is the cheapest self-check in this section.
REJECT ROOTS OUTSIDE THE SUPPORT: solving $F(m)=0.5$ usually gives a quadratic or cubic with one admissible root. Show the rejection and its reason in the working.

EVERY ITEM CARRIES A `[tikz]` FIGURE of the density with the measure marked in the SOLUTION figure only (the median line, the mode's peak) — never on the question figure. Plot as restricted function plots clipped to the axis window; never `^` inside a plotted expression.
The shipped Standard skills `median-from-data`, `quartiles` and `mode` own data-based measures. Every item here must work from a DENSITY, never from a list of values.

sections.name: normal-distribution-advanced
hazards: SEVEN NORMAL-DISTRIBUTION SKILLS ARE GENERATED IN W4-3 AT THE STANDARD LEVEL — `normal-distribution-shape`, `calculate-z-score`, `z-score-to-raw-score`, `compare-z-scores`, `empirical-rule`, `normal-probabilities` and `z-table-probability`. This section covers ONLY what Advanced adds on top, and must not re-teach any of them.

One routine per skill. `normal-distribution-features` = the curve as a probability DENSITY — total area $1$, symmetry about $\mu$, the points of inflection at $\mu\pm\sigma$, and the effect of changing $\mu$ (translation) or $\sigma$ (width and height) on the curve's shape. `standard-normal-distribution` = why $Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}$ has $\mu=0$ and $\sigma=1$, and that ANY normal variable maps to the same standard curve. `normal-mean-sd-from-probability` = the REVERSE problem — given $P(X<c)$ and one of $\mu$ or $\sigma$, find the other by inverting to a $z$ value first.

THE POINTS OF INFLECTION SIT AT $\mu\pm\sigma$, not at $\mu\pm2\sigma$ and not at the mean. That fact is the distinguishing content of `normal-distribution-features`; make the wrong positions named distractors.

A LARGER $\sigma$ MAKES THE CURVE WIDER AND LOWER — the total area stays $1$, so the peak must fall. 'Drew a wider curve at the same height' is a compulsory named distractor, and any comparison figure must show both curves with visibly different peak heights.

IN `normal-mean-sd-from-probability` THE $z$ VALUE IS FOUND FIRST AND ITS SIGN IS DECIDED BY WHICH SIDE OF THE MEAN $c$ LIES: $P(X<c)=0.2$ means $z$ is NEGATIVE. Getting that sign wrong is the compulsory named distractor, and at least half the items must have a probability below $0.5$. Solve $c=\mu+z\sigma$ for the unknown and substitute back to check the probability comes out right before keying.

EVERY ITEM CARRIES A `[tikz]` BELL CURVE. Plot it as a function using `exp(-x*x/2)`-style expressions — NEVER `^` inside a plotted TikZ expression — clipped to the axis window at about $\pm4$, with the axis ticked at the $z$ or $x$ values the item names. Where two curves are compared, draw both on one set of axes with the equations labelled OFF the curves.
Any table this section needs is a KaTeX `array` inside `$…$`, never [tikz].

sections.name: bernoulli
hazards: One routine per skill. `bernoulli-random-variable` = a single trial with exactly two outcomes, $P(X=1)=p$ and $P(X=0)=1-p$, and identifying whether a described situation IS Bernoulli. `bernoulli-mean-variance` = $E(X)=p$ and $\mathrm{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$, including deriving them from the discrete definitions. `bernoulli-applications` = using a Bernoulli model in context, including a sequence of independent Bernoulli trials treated one at a time.

A BERNOULLI VARIABLE HAS EXACTLY ONE TRIAL. The moment an item counts successes over $n$ trials it is binomial and belongs to the next section — keep that line strict, since it is the only thing separating these three skills from their neighbours.

$\mathrm{Var}(X)=p(1-p)$ IS MAXIMISED AT $p=0.5$ and is never negative. Include one item asking for the $p$ that maximises the variance, and check every computed variance lies in $[0,0.25]$ before keying.
'SUCCESS' IS WHATEVER THE STEM DEFINES, and it need not be the good outcome. Include at least one item where success is a defect or a failure, and make 'used $1-p$ as $p$' a named distractor.

A SITUATION WITHOUT INDEPENDENCE OR WITH MORE THAN TWO OUTCOMES IS NOT BERNOULLI. `bernoulli-random-variable` must include an item whose correct answer is that the model does not apply, with the reason named.
This section is figure-free: emit no [tikz] blocks. A two-row probability table is a KaTeX `array` inside `$…$`.

sections.name: binomial-distribution
hazards: One routine per skill. `binomial-random-variable` = the four conditions (fixed $n$, two outcomes, constant $p$, independent trials), the notation $X\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$, and judging whether a situation qualifies. `binomial-probability-formula` = $P(X=r)=\binom{n}{r}p^{r}(1-p)^{n-r}$ for a single value of $r$. `binomial-mean-variance` = $E(X)=np$, $\mathrm{Var}(X)=np(1-p)$, $\sigma=\sqrt{np(1-p)}$, and reverse problems (find $n$ or $p$ from the mean and variance).

THE EXPONENTS MUST SUM TO $n$: $p^{r}(1-p)^{n-r}$. Swapping them, or using $p^{n-r}$, is the compulsory named distractor for `binomial-probability-formula`, and at least one item must have $r$ close to but not equal to $\frac{n}{2}$ so the swap changes the value.

SAMPLING WITHOUT REPLACEMENT FROM A SMALL POPULATION IS NOT BINOMIAL — $p$ changes between trials. `binomial-random-variable` must include such an item with 'not binomial, because the trials are not independent' as the correct response.

$\mathrm{Var}=np(1-p)$, NOT $np^{2}$ AND NOT $\sqrt{np}$. The reverse problem (given $\mu=12$ and $\sigma^{2}=4.8$, find $n$ and $p$) is solved by dividing: $\frac{\sigma^{2}}{\mu}=1-p$. Include it, and check the resulting $n$ is a positive INTEGER and $p\in(0,1)$ — if not, the item is broken.

RECOMPUTE EVERY BINOMIAL PROBABILITY digit by digit and confirm it lies in $[0,1]$ and that the probabilities you offer as options are not accidentally equal. Pin the rounding in every stem ('to 4 decimal places') so two options cannot both be defensible.

A probability HISTOGRAM for $\mathrm{Bin}(n,p)$ is a legitimate `[tikz]` display for `binomial-random-variable` — a bar chart following the data-displays anti-collision rules, with the bar heights actually equal to the computed probabilities. Verify each bar's height against the formula; a histogram whose bars contradict the distribution is the figure-vs-answer defect class.
`combinations-nCr` shipped in W3-9 and is assumed — do not re-teach counting. But $\binom{n}{r}$ must be evaluated correctly in every solution; recompute each one.

sections.name: binomial-applications
hazards: One routine per skill. `binomial-expected-frequency` = the expected NUMBER of trials/groups producing a given outcome, $N\times P(X=r)$ or $np$ — a count, not a probability. `binomial-cumulative-probability` = $P(X\le r)$, $P(X\ge r)$ and $P(a\le X\le b)$ by summing terms, including the complement shortcut. `solve-binomial-problems` = multi-step applied problems that choose the model, compute and interpret.

'AT LEAST ONE' IS $1-P(X=0)$ — the complement is the whole technique and must be the compulsory named structural type of `binomial-cumulative-probability`. 'At least $r$' is $1-P(X\le r-1)$: the OFF-BY-ONE on that boundary is the compulsory named distractor, and every cumulative stem must be unambiguous about whether the endpoint is included.

SUM EVERY CUMULATIVE PROBABILITY TERM BY TERM AND RE-ADD IT. This is the batch's hot spot for arithmetic in prose; write each $\binom{n}{r}p^{r}(1-p)^{n-r}$ term on its own line, then the sum, and confirm the total lies in $[0,1]$.

AN EXPECTED FREQUENCY IS A COUNT and rounds to a whole number of items only when the stem asks for a practical count; the unrounded expected value may legitimately be non-integer. Pin which is wanted in every stem, and never place a probability and a count in one option list.

$P(X\le r)$ AND $P(X<r)$ DIFFER FOR A DISCRETE VARIABLE — unlike the continuous case. Say which in every stem; this is exactly the boundary the continuous sections of this batch treat the other way, so the contrast must be explicit.
This section is figure-free: emit no [tikz] blocks.

Give each of the three skills its own context family (quality control, multiple-choice guessing, medical screening, sport, manufacturing) and check no two items across all six binomial/Bernoulli skills share a value signature — $n$, $p$ and $r$ collide easily across sibling skills.
